President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, declaring Saturday that the United States was winning.
“Well I’m rejecting their deal,” Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Tennessee.
The blunt response came after Tehran proposed reopening the waterway within seven days in exchange for major American concessions.
Iran wanted the U.S. naval blockade lifted, sanctions on its oil sales waived and a ceasefire covering Lebanon.
Its proposal also called for nuclear negotiations to resume on an accelerated schedule.
Trump argued that Iran’s request showed economic pressure was working and Tehran needed money from oil exports.
The blockade and sanctions have squeezed Iran’s finances, increasing Tehran’s incentive to seek a quick deal.
He said Iran wanted to open the strait immediately because it was losing badly.
“We’re winning tremendously,” the president said while describing American control over the strategic shipping route.
Trump asserted that 29 ships had passed through the waterway the previous night.
He said he remained open to reaching an agreement, but insisted the terms Iran offered were unacceptable.
The president portrayed his naval blockade as a direct response to Iran’s interference with shipping.
He called the blockade a “wall of steel” and said it prevented Tehran from profiting while others could pass.
Washington says commercial shipping can continue through Hormuz even as Iranian ports remain under the U.S. blockade.
Trump argued that Iran had tried to create a global crisis by shutting the route.
Instead, he said, the U.S. operation left Iran unable to collect the revenue it expected.
The Strait of Hormuz carried about one-fifth of globally traded oil and gas before the war.
Its disruption has affected energy markets well beyond the Middle East and raised costs for consumers.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the latest offer during a private gathering at the United Nations.
The proposal reached Washington through mediators, according to accounts of the negotiations.
It resembled a June understanding but replaced its 60-day interim period with a seven-day timeline.
That earlier arrangement collapsed after Iran resumed attacks on shipping in the strait.
Trump’s answer makes clear he is unwilling to exchange immediate relief for the reopening Tehran offered.
It does not mean the administration has ruled out every possible future agreement with Iran.
Before his remarks, Trump posted that Iran cannot be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
That longstanding American demand remains central to any broader talks over Tehran’s nuclear program.
The president spoke while heading to a Tennessee football game involving the Volunteers and Texas Longhorns.
His comments followed a Wall Street Journal report that he had already turned down the Iranian proposal.
The Journal also reported Trump expected to resume bombing Iran after the November midterm elections.
Trump did not announce such a plan in the remarks reported Saturday.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian separately said his country had little trust in Washington during an Al-Jazeera interview.
He argued that security in the strait must be achieved through negotiations rather than a regional enforcer.
Pezeshkian said Qatar and Pakistan were among the third parties conveying messages between Iran and the United States.
Other Gulf governments have also been involved in efforts to prevent further escalation.
Saudi Arabia reportedly has reservations about a deal that leaves threats to Red Sea shipping unresolved.
Iran-backed Houthi fighters have increased pressure around the Bab el-Mandeb strait near Yemen.
The possible inclusion of Lebanon in a ceasefire would add another complication to any agreement.
Hard-liners inside Iran have also criticized the diplomatic approach taken by Pezeshkian and Araghchi.
Some favor continuing or escalating the conflict to demand greater concessions from Washington.
The White House had described conversations with mediators as positive and constructive before Trump’s public rejection, The Wall Street Journal reported.
For now, the president is betting that the blockade gives Washington stronger negotiating power.
This article may contain commentary which reflects the author's opinion.

President Trump just rejected Iran’s seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz—and once you see what Tehran demanded up front, his answer makes a lot more sense.
Iran offered to restore normal passage through the vital waterway and restart nuclear negotiations within a week. But the offer came with a massive price tag: Washington would first have to unwind the very pressure that brought Tehran back to the table.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Saturday, President Trump did not hedge.
“I reject their proposal,” he said. “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly.”

Trump has rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day roadmap that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart negotiations. Trump told reporters plainly: “I reject their proposal.”
— The Golden Age (@QAceofTruth) September 27, 2026
The word “proposal” makes Tehran’s plan sound like a simple ceasefire offer. It was anything but simple.
According to Al Jazeera, Iran wanted the United States to end its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release frozen Iranian funds, and observe a regional ceasefire that would extend to Lebanon and Yemen.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said those American steps could be completed in four or five days. Only then, on the seventh day, would Iran reopen the strait and begin negotiations over a final agreement.
That sequence is the heart of the dispute.
Tehran was not offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz first and then negotiate relief based on compliance. It was asking the United States to surrender economic and military leverage before Iran delivered its central promise.
The frozen-assets demand alone reportedly involved roughly $12 billion. Add restored oil revenue, an end to the blockade, and a ceasefire reaching beyond Iran’s borders, and the proposed opening of the strait begins to look less like a concession than a costly transaction.
That matters because the Strait of Hormuz is not an ordinary shipping lane. Roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the world’s oil normally moves through the narrow passage, according to The Washington Post.
Iran mined the waterway and warned ships against passing without coordinating with Tehran after the war began in February. Traffic collapsed, energy costs surged, and the strait became Tehran’s most powerful bargaining chip.
The resulting pressure is not confined to the Persian Gulf. Restricted shipping has driven up fuel costs around the world, meaning Tehran’s control of the chokepoint reaches directly into household budgets, freight rates, and the price of moving nearly everything.
That gives both sides a reason to negotiate, but it also raises the stakes of the sequence. If Washington delivers sanctions relief and releases frozen assets first, it may have fewer tools left if Tehran delays the reopening or attaches new conditions on day seven.
But the pressure has not moved in only one direction.
President Trump’s administration imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports while the Treasury Department launched Operation Economic Outcast—a worldwide campaign aimed at cutting off the regime’s oil revenue, banking channels, aviation access, shipping support, and sanctions-evasion networks.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that the United States had dispatched teams around the globe to press governments into action against the Iranian regime.
Following the launch of Operation Economic Outcast, @USTreasury imposed targeted financial measures against banks and aviation service providers. At my direction, teams were dispatched across the globe to engage with countries and demand action against the Iranian regime.
— Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (@SecScottBessent) September 26, 2026
The administration’s theory is straightforward: Iran should not receive sanctions relief merely for promising to stop obstructing a waterway it helped close.
The Treasury Department said its latest aviation sanctions hit 36 targets, including Iranian airlines, front companies, foreign intermediaries, and procurement networks. Treasury warned that foreign firms enabling sanctioned Iranian aviation could be cut off from the U.S. financial system.
In other words, the economic squeeze is not a slogan. It is a coordinated attempt to make every bank, carrier, port, supplier, and government choose between access to the American financial system and business with Tehran.
Iran’s sudden seven-day timetable arrived against that backdrop.
Araghchi said Tehran would not back down from its conditions and was waiting for a formal answer through Qatari mediators. President Trump, meanwhile, said he remains willing to make a deal—just not this deal.
That distinction matters. Rejecting an unacceptable offer is not the same as rejecting diplomacy.
The White House continues to frame the confrontation around a larger objective: preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon while denying the regime the resources it uses to threaten the United States and its allies.
.@USAmbUN: “Politics have nothing to do with this. This is about keeping the next generation safe from Iran threatening the world with a nuclear weapon.”
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) September 27, 2026
President Trump now faces a difficult balance. Keeping the strait restricted carries real costs for American families and the global economy.
Accepting Tehran’s terms, however, could restore billions of dollars and vital revenue to the regime before it has reopened the waterway or signed a durable nuclear agreement.
A seven-day countdown sounds fast. The fine print showed that nearly every meaningful American concession would come before Iran’s promised performance.
That is why Tehran’s offer was rejected—and why the next proposal will have to be more than a demand for relief wrapped around a promise to talk.

President Donald Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations, hours after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented the plan at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Friday.
The proposal would have started a seven-day process leading to the reopening of the strategic waterway and the resumption of talks.
Trump told reporters on Saturday that he rejected the proposal, arguing that Tehran was seeking an agreement while under pressure from the conflict.
"I reject their proposal," he told reporters.
He added, "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they're losing so badly. We're winning tremendously. They want to make a deal, and I think that's fine. I like making a deal too, but that deal would not be acceptable."
The rejection came as Iran continued to call for negotiations. Iranian officials said the proposal had been conveyed to Washington through mediators, including Qatar, although Tehran was still awaiting a formal U.S. response through diplomatic channels, according to reports.
Iran Offers Seven-Day Strait Reopening Plan
Araghchi said Friday that Iran was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restore normal maritime passage within seven days if Washington accepted Tehran's conditions.
"If certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will be open at the end of seven days, and talks will be restarted," Araghchi said.
He later told reporters at the U.N., "If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States."
Iran's conditions included lifting the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports, easing restrictions on Iranian oil sales and observing a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Araghchi said the initial steps could be completed within four or five days, with the waterway reopening by the sixth day and negotiations beginning on the seventh day.
The proposal linked two issues that Washington and Tehran have been negotiating, restoring maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and restarting talks on a broader political settlement.
The Nuclear Issue Remains a Central Dispute
Iran's nuclear program remains one of the most difficult issues in negotiations.
Trump has repeatedly said Iran cannot acquire a nuclear weapon. On Saturday, he reiterated that position in a post on his Truth Social account. "IRAN CAN NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!!!"
The United States and Iran had already addressed the nuclear issue in their June memorandum of understanding, but the document left major questions for negotiations. The agreement established a 60-day negotiation period and deferred several difficult issues, including the long-term treatment of Iran's nuclear program.
The June framework included Iranian commitments relating to its nuclear activities, while the United States was expected to take steps involving sanctions and its naval blockade. The arrangement also contemplated further negotiations over how Iran's enriched uranium would be handled.
Trump has separately said the United States will not allow Iran to retain its nuclear material.
"We will get it. We don't need it, we don't want it. We'll probably destroy it after we get it, but we're not going to let them have it," Trump told reporters.
Iran has maintained that it will not surrender what it describes as its sovereign rights.
"Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," Araghchi said.
June Deal Left Key Issues Unresolved
The latest proposal also builds on an earlier diplomatic framework.
In June, the United States and Iran reached a memorandum of understanding that provided for 60 days of negotiations toward a broader agreement. The framework included provisions concerning the Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. naval blockade and Iran's nuclear activities, while leaving several detailed issues for the negotiations.
The arrangement established a framework for negotiations but left unresolved questions about the sequencing of U.S. and Iranian actions.
Iran's new proposal makes the reopening of the Strait conditional on steps by Washington, while Trump has rejected the proposed terms rather than accepting the seven-day process.
U.S.-Iran Talks Face Major Unresolved Disputes
A U.S. official previously said Washington and Tehran were continuing discussions through mediators, with the nuclear issue among the subjects under negotiation. Trump said talks with Iran were continuing while maintaining that Tehran could not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has likewise said Tehran remains prepared for dialogue while rejecting what he describes as coercion.
"Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock," Pezeshkian said at the U.N.
The key disputes remain centered on the conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. sanctions and blockade measures, and the future of Iran's nuclear program.

Just days after he was threatening to annihilate Iran to the UN General Assembly, it is stunning that Trump is now claiming he's rejecting an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
As The Guardian reported, it was more of the same old song and dance we've been hearing from him since he dragged us into this quagmire earlier this year:
Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations general assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state.
Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran, which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
The Iranians responded to Trump's threats by telling him they'll never "bend the knee":
President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Iran will never "bend the knee" after almost seven months of war with the US and Israel, but is ready for a diplomatic solution to the conflict.
Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, he told the UN General Assembly: "The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying."
Pezeshkian also insisted any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using a key Gulf waterway.
"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access," he said.
There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address.
Now Trump is claiming he's rejected a deal with them:
Speaking to reporters Saturday as he departed the White House for Tennessee, where he is expected to attend a college football contest between the Texas Longhorns and the Tennessee Volunteers, Trump appeared to confirm an earlier report from The Wall Street Journal which said he had already refused the deal.
“Well I’m rejecting their deal,” Trump said.
“They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” the president continued. “You know you don’t read that, you don’t see that in the fake news.
“We’re winning tremendously. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait, massive amounts of oil are coming out of the Hormuz Strait,” he said.
“Last night we had 29 ships come out. They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine, I like making a deal, too, but that deal would not be acceptable,” Trump added.
“And what they want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait. You know why? Because they’re dying,” Trump said. “You know why they’re dying? Because they have no money coming in. Because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait.
“So they outsmarted themselves. They said, ‘Let’s close it and cause a problem for the world.’ And then I came along and we put up the greatest blockade ever in military history. It’s a wall of steel.”
“I would put it up and guess what? They don’t have any money now because they wanted to close the strait. And I said, ‘That’s fine, we’re going to close it on you. But everybody else is able to use it,’” Trump continued.
The Iranians know they can't trust Trump to honor any deal they might make.
